etymology: Hebrew leb (לֵב) and lebab (לֵבָב) — the inner core of the person.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for heart, but vastly broader than the modern English emotional sense. Leb is the seat of thought, will, conscience, memory, and decision — the integrated inner core of the person. "Out of the heart proceed" (Matt 15:19) every kind of thought, not just feelings.
webster_summary: Hebrew "heart" — the integrated inner core of the person.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for heart (leb, or the doubled emphatic form lebab) is the integrated seat of inner life: thought, will, conscience, memory, decision, affection. Where modern English splits "heart" (feelings) from "mind" (thought), Hebrew unites them in leb. To love YHWH "with all thy heart" (Deut 6:5) is to love Him with the integrated inner self — thinking, willing, remembering, deciding, feeling all toward Him.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 6:5
And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.
Proverbs 4:23
Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Jeremiah 17:9
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?
corruption_summary: Modern English splits heart (feelings) from mind (thought); Hebrew leb unites them, and the modern split distorts the biblical anthropology.
corruption_paragraphs: Pop usage of "follow your heart" treats the heart as feelings-organ to be obeyed. Hebrew leb includes the will, the conscience, and the deliberative reasoning — and Jeremiah 17:9 warns that this integrated core is deceitful and desperately wicked. Following your leb uncritically is bad counsel.

Recover the integration: when Scripture says "with all thy heart" it means with the whole inner person — not just feelings. The heart is what God renews ("a new heart will I give you," Ezek 36:26), and the renewal touches every faculty.
usage: Heart (leb) is thought + will + conscience + feeling.
Don't follow your leb uncritically; let it be renewed.
Love God with the integrated inner self.

etymology: Hebrew chokmah (חָכְמָה) — skill, expertise, wisdom; the practical-spiritual ability to live rightly.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for wisdom — not abstract knowledge but practical-spiritual skill at living. The same word names the bezalel-skill of tabernacle craftsmen (Exod 31:3) and the moral-spiritual wisdom of Proverbs. Wisdom is craftsmanship of the soul.
webster_summary: Hebrew "wisdom" — practical-spiritual skill at living rightly.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for wisdom is broader than abstract knowledge. Chokmah names the practical-spiritual skill of the craftsman (Bezalel filled with the Spirit of God in chokmah for tabernacle work, Exod 31:3) and the moral-spiritual skill of right living (Proverbs). Wisdom is craftsmanship applied to soul, household, business, and worship.
scriptures: Proverbs 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
Proverbs 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Exodus 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge.
corruption_summary: Reduced to abstract intellectual category; the practical-craftsmanship sense of chokmah is dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "wisdom" sounds intellectual — the philosopher's commodity. Hebrew chokmah includes the craftsman's hand-skill: the seamstress, the metalworker, the woodworker filled with the Spirit. Wisdom is doing rightly, not just thinking rightly.
Recover the craftsmanship: chokmah is for the kitchen, the workshop, the field, the household. The fear of the LORD is the beginning — the rest is hand-trained skill.
usage: Chokmah is hand-skill, not just brain-skill.
Bezalel had it; so did the Proverbs sage.
Fear of the LORD is the beginning.

etymology: Hebrew binah (בִּינָה) — from bin, to discern, separate, distinguish; insight that distinguishes between things.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for understanding — specifically insight that distinguishes, separates, weighs. Distinct from chokmah (skill) and daath (knowledge), binah is the discriminating faculty that tells truth from lie, good from evil, wisdom from folly.
webster_summary: Hebrew "understanding" — the discriminating faculty.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for understanding, distinct from wisdom (chokmah, skill) and knowledge (daath, acquaintance). Binah is the discerning faculty — the ability to tell things apart, to weigh, to distinguish between cases. Solomon prayed for binah when he asked God for an understanding heart to judge the people.
scriptures: 1 Kings 3:9
Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad.
Proverbs 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Isaiah 11:2
And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might.
corruption_summary: Conflated with general intellectual understanding; the discriminating, between-good-and-bad force is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "understanding" can mean empathy, comprehension, or vague familiarity. Hebrew binah is sharper: the faculty that distinguishes truth from lie. Solomon's prayer was for moral-judicial discernment, not warm sympathy.
Recover the sharpness: pray for binah as the ability to tell the difference between things that look similar — true gospel and false, real love and counterfeit, wisdom and rationalized folly.
usage: Binah distinguishes; chokmah does.
Solomon prayed for binah to judge.
The Spirit of binah rests on the Messiah.

etymology: Hebrew tsedaqah (צְדָקָה), feminine of tsedeq — rightness, justice, conformity to a standard.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for righteousness, a relational-covenantal concept rather than abstract moral perfection. Tsedaqah is right-relating — faithful to covenant obligations, just in dealings, generous to the poor (in later usage almsgiving). YHWH's tsedaqah is His covenant faithfulness expressed as saving action.
webster_summary: Hebrew "righteousness" — relational covenant-faithfulness.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for righteousness, broader than abstract moral standing. Tsedaqah is right-relating: faithful to covenant obligations, just in dealings, generous to the poor (tzedakah in later Jewish usage means almsgiving precisely because giving to the poor is part of being righteous). YHWH's tsedaqah is His own covenant faithfulness expressed as saving action toward His people.
scriptures: Genesis 15:6
And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
Isaiah 51:5-6
My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth... my righteousness shall not be abolished.
Micah 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: Reduced to private moral correctness; the covenantal-relational depth and the included-justice for the poor get lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "righteousness" sounds private and moralistic — clean-living. Hebrew tsedaqah includes how you treat the widow, the orphan, the sojourner, the worker. There is no private righteousness in the prophets — right-relating to God is inseparable from right-relating to your neighbor.
Recover the covenant-frame: tsedaqah is faithfulness in relationship. The God whose tsedaqah is His covenant faithfulness expects His people's tsedaqah to look like covenant faithfulness too.
usage: Tsedaqah is right-relating, not private morality.
YHWH's tsedaqah is His saving covenant faithfulness.
Almsgiving is righteousness in the Hebrew frame.

etymology: Hebrew yirah (יִרְאָה), from yare — to fear, reverence, stand in awe.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for fear, especially "fear of the LORD." Not anxious dread but reverent awe leading to obedience. The beginning of wisdom (Prov 9:10), the first commandment of the Shema's love (Deut 6:5 implies it), and the disposition that recognizes God for who He is.
webster_summary: Hebrew "fear" — reverent awe of YHWH.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for fear, especially in the construct "fear of the LORD" (yirat YHWH). Not anxious dread but reverent awe that recognizes God for who He is — holy, sovereign, just, gracious — and responds with worship and obedience. The beginning of wisdom; the disposition that orients all of life rightly.
scriptures: Proverbs 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Ecclesiastes 12:13
Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.
Psalm 34:11
Come, ye children, hearken unto me: I will teach you the fear of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Modern Christianity often softens "fear of the LORD" into mere respect, losing the reverent-awe weight Scripture intends.
corruption_paragraphs: "God is love, why fear?" goes the modern softening. Scripture binds the two together: God's love is His holy love, and reverent awe of His holiness is the beginning of wisdom. To shrink yirah to respect is to lose the awe that makes worship possible.
Recover the awe: yirah is not abusive-relationship dread; it is the saint's right-orientation before the holy God. The same God whose chesed is unfailing is the God whose holiness consumes.
usage: Yirah is reverent awe, not abusive dread.
The beginning of wisdom is fear of the LORD.
Recover awe; worship grows from it.

etymology: Hebrew tikvah (תִּקְוָה), from qavah (to wait, expect) — literally "a waiting," "a cord" (the line of expectation).
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for hope. From the verb qavah (to wait), tikvah is sustained expectation rooted in God's character — not wishful optimism. The same word means "cord" (Josh 2:18, Rahab's scarlet line) — hope is the cord that connects present darkness to promised deliverance.
webster_summary: Hebrew "hope" — sustained expectation rooted in God.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for hope, derived from qavah (to wait, expect). Tikvah is the sustained, oriented expectation of those who trust God's promises. Curiously the same word can mean "cord" or "line" (Rahab's scarlet thread, Josh 2:18) — hope is the cord that connects present darkness to promised deliverance. The Israeli national anthem is named Hatikvah, "the hope."
scriptures: Jeremiah 29:11
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end (tikvah).
Psalm 62:5
My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation (tikvah) is from him.
Lamentations 3:21-23
This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope. It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed... they are new every morning.
corruption_summary: Reduced to optimism or wishful thinking; the sustained, God-rooted expectation that survives Lamentations gets lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "hope" is often optimistic feeling. Hebrew tikvah survived Lamentations — the destruction of Jerusalem, the exile, the temple's burning. "This I recall... therefore have I hope" (Lam 3:21). Hope is what stands when optimism has nothing to cling to.
Recover the cord-image: hope is the line that connects ruin to restoration. Rahab's scarlet thread saved her household; tikvah is the saint's scarlet thread through every dark season.
usage: Tikvah is sustained expectation, not wishful feeling.
Hope is the cord through Lamentations.
Israel's anthem: HaTikvah, the hope.

etymology: Hebrew batach (בָּטַח) — to trust, lean upon, feel safe in.
biblical_def: The Hebrew verb for trust. Different from aman (to be firm, the root of amen and emunah): batach emphasizes the felt-security of leaning on something solid. To trust YHWH is to lean your weight on Him with the felt-confidence that He will hold.
webster_summary: Hebrew "trust" — to lean with felt-security on YHWH.
webster_full: The Hebrew verb most often translated "trust." Distinguished from aman (firmness, faithfulness, the root of amen): batach emphasizes the felt-security of leaning. To batach in YHWH is to throw your weight on Him with confidence He will not give way. The opposite is to trust horses, princes, riches — supports that buckle.
scriptures: Psalm 56:3
What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
Proverbs 3:5-6
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Isaiah 26:3-4
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee. Trust ye in the LORD for ever: for in the LORD JEHOVAH is everlasting strength.
corruption_summary: Reduced to general optimism ("trust the universe," "trust the process") rather than the specific lean-on-YHWH the verb commands.
corruption_paragraphs: The age has generic "trust" — trust your gut, trust the science, trust the universe. Scripture is specific: trust YHWH. Other supports buckle. Horses fall, princes die, riches fly. Only the LORD holds when leaned on with full weight.
Recover the felt-security: batach is leaning. Throw your weight; He holds.
usage: Batach is leaning with felt-security.
Trust YHWH; other supports buckle.
Throw your weight; He holds.

etymology: Hebrew nacham (נָחַם) — to sigh, breathe deeply, comfort, regret.
biblical_def: A double-meaning Hebrew verb: to comfort (give breathing-room to the distressed) and to relent / regret (change of mind from grief). YHWH comforts His people in Isa 40:1; YHWH "repented" (relented) over judgment in Jonah 3:10. The verb pictures the deep breath of relief or grief.
webster_summary: Hebrew "comfort" / "relent" — the deep breath of relief or grief.
webster_full: The Hebrew verb that means both to comfort (the deep breath of relief given to the distressed) and to relent or regret (the deep breath of grief that turns from a path). Same verb. YHWH nachams His people (Isa 40:1) and nachams over judgment when Nineveh repents (Jonah 3:10). The breathing-image is the link.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:1
Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God.
Jonah 3:10
And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented (nacham) of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.
Genesis 5:29
And he called his name Noah (related to nacham), saying, This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil.
corruption_summary: The double-sense (comfort + relent) gets lost in English translations that pick one rendering or the other.
corruption_paragraphs: English translators must pick: comfort or repent. The Hebrew didn't pick — the same breath that gives relief turns from judgment. The God who relents from threatened judgment is the God who comforts His penitent people. Same breath; same character.
Recover the unified verb: when YHWH nachams, He breathes deeply — toward His people in tenderness, away from His own threatened wrath in mercy. Both are nacham.
usage: Nacham is the deep-breath verb — comfort or relent.
Same breath that comforts also turns from judgment.
Read Isa 40 and Jonah 3 together.

etymology: Hebrew oz (עֹז) — strength, might, fierceness; the personal-protective strength of YHWH.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for strength, especially YHWH's saving strength on behalf of His people. Distinguished from gevurah (raw might) and chayil (force / valor). Oz is fierce protective strength — what a mother shows for her children, what YHWH shows for the saint.
webster_summary: Hebrew "strength" — fierce protective might.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for strength, distinct from gevurah (raw might) and chayil (force, valor, virtue). Oz is fierce protective strength — the strength that defends and shields. Used of YHWH's saving strength on behalf of His people, of the king's strength, and of the woman of valor (Prov 31:25).
scriptures: Psalm 28:7
The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped.
Psalm 29:11
The LORD will give strength unto his people; the LORD will bless his people with peace.
Proverbs 31:25
Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
corruption_summary: Reduced to abstract "strength" without the protective-fierce shading of the Hebrew.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "strength" can mean tough, capable, athletic. Hebrew oz shades toward fierce-protective — the lioness for her cubs, YHWH for His people, the Proverbs 31 woman whose strength clothes her.
Recover the protection: oz is for those defended by it. The strength of the LORD is for His people; her strength is for her household.
usage: Oz is fierce protective strength.
The LORD's oz is for His people.
Strength clothes the Proverbs 31 woman.

etymology: Hebrew gevurah (גְּבוּרָה), from gabar (to be strong, prevail) — might, mighty deeds, prevailing power.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for might or mighty acts — the prevailing-power side of God's character. Distinguished from oz (protective strength), gevurah is the raw might that breaks armies and rolls back seas. The plural gevurot (mighty deeds) names YHWH's saving acts in history.
webster_summary: Hebrew "might" — raw prevailing power; mighty deeds.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for raw might, prevailing power, mighty deeds. Distinguished from oz (protective strength) and chayil (valor): gevurah emphasizes overwhelming, breaking-through power. The plural gevurot denotes YHWH's mighty acts — creation, exodus, conquest, resurrection. The Spirit of gevurah rests on the Messiah (Isa 11:2).
scriptures: They shall speak of the glory of thy kingdom, and talk of thy power; To make known to the sons of men his mighty acts (gevurot).
Isaiah 11:2
And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might (gevurah).
With him is wisdom and strength, he hath counsel and understanding.
corruption_summary: Conflated with abstract power; the specific raw-prevailing force of gevurah and its connection to YHWH's mighty saving deeds gets thinned.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern usage of "might" is generic. Hebrew gevurah is specific: the raw prevailing power that breaks Pharaoh's armies, parts the Red Sea, brings dry bones to life. The Spirit of gevurah rests on the Messiah; the same Spirit raises the saints.
Recover the saving-deed framework: gevurah is the verb of YHWH's interventions. We tell stories of His gevurot. The exodus, the resurrection, the new birth — all gevurah.
usage: Gevurah is raw prevailing power.
Tell the gevurot — YHWH's mighty deeds.
Spirit of gevurah on the Messiah.

etymology: Hebrew magen (מָגֵן) — small round shield, defense; figuratively, divine protection.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for shield (specifically the small round shield carried in personal combat). Used metaphorically of YHWH as the defender of His people: "the LORD is my shield" (Ps 28:7). The Star of David is called Magen David — the shield of David, since David's psalms repeatedly name YHWH as his shield.
webster_summary: Hebrew "shield" — YHWH as personal defense.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for the small round shield carried in personal combat. Used extensively as metaphor for YHWH's defense of His people. The phrase magen David ("the shield of David") gives the modern Star of David its name — rooted in David's repeated declaration in the Psalms that YHWH was his shield.
scriptures: Genesis 15:1
Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.
Psalm 28:7
The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped.
Psalm 84:11
For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
corruption_summary: Modern usage of "shield" is mostly metaphorical and generic; the specific personal-combat image and the YHWH-as-shield identification have thinned.
corruption_paragraphs: When you say "shield" today, you might think credit-card protection or sun-shield. The biblical image is the small round shield carried close to the body in personal combat. YHWH is that shield — not distant protection, but in-the-fight defense.
Recover the personal closeness: magen is at-hand defense, not policy or insurance. The LORD is my shield — right here, right now, between me and the blow.
usage: Magen is at-hand personal defense.
The LORD is my shield — in the fight.
Magen David: the Shield of David.

etymology: Hebrew tsur (צוּר) — rock, cliff, stronghold; the immovable foundation.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for rock, especially used as a divine title. Tsur is the great cliff-face, the strong-rock, the immovable foundation. "He is the Rock, his work is perfect" (Deut 32:4). Distinct from even (a stone). Christ is the spiritual Rock that followed Israel (1 Cor 10:4).
webster_summary: Hebrew "rock" — YHWH as immovable foundation.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for rock, especially the large cliff or stronghold-rock (distinct from even, a stone). Used extensively as a divine title: "the LORD is my rock" (Ps 18:2). The Song of Moses calls God "the Rock" repeatedly (Deut 32). Paul identifies the rock that gave water in the wilderness as Christ (1 Cor 10:4).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:4
He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.
Psalm 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust.
1 Corinthians 10:4
And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a stable-image without the cliff-face / stronghold-rock force the Hebrew carries; the divine-title weight thinned.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "rock" suggests pebble or boulder. Hebrew tsur suggests cliff-face, stronghold, immovable bulk. When the Song of Moses calls God "the Rock," the picture is the great stone wall in the desert — you can climb it, hide behind it, build on it.
Recover the bulk: YHWH is not pebble-stable; He is cliff-stable. Christ is the Rock that gave water in the wilderness — the same Rock that follows the saints across all the deserts.
usage: Tsur is cliff-face, stronghold-rock.
Christ is the Rock that follows.
Build on the Rock; hide in the Rock.

etymology: Hebrew machseh (מַחֲסֶה), from chasah (to take refuge, flee for shelter).
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for refuge — a place of shelter and retreat in danger. Chasah (the verb) is the saint's instinctive run to YHWH for cover. Psalm 91 is the great refuge-psalm: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."
webster_summary: Hebrew "refuge" — place of shelter; YHWH as cover.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for refuge or shelter; the place to which one flees in danger. Derived from chasah, to take cover. Used frequently of YHWH as the saint's place of safety: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble" (Ps 46:1). The cities of refuge in Mosaic law (arei miqlat) used a different word but expressed the same theological category.
scriptures: Psalm 46:1
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Psalm 91:2
I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
Proverbs 14:26
In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge.
corruption_summary: Modern "refuge" carries displaced-person connotations; the active-running-for-shelter sense of chasah/machseh is dimmer.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "refuge" is mostly political (refugee crises). Hebrew machseh is active and personal: I am running for shelter; YHWH is my cover. The verb chasah is what doves do under wings (Ps 91:4). The saint takes cover in the LORD.
Recover the run: refuge is not residence; it is escape-to-cover. When the storm comes, run to the Rock. Machseh is the running and the place run-to.
roots_lines: to take refuge, flee for shelter
usage: Machseh is active running-to-shelter.
Chasah under His wings.
Storm comes; run to the Rock.

etymology: Hebrew metsudah (מְצוּדָה) — mountain stronghold, fortress; the heavily-fortified high place.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for fortress, specifically a mountain stronghold. David hid in metsudoth (strongholds) when fleeing Saul (1 Sam 22:4-5; 23:14). The word becomes a divine title in the Psalms: "the LORD is my rock, and my fortress" (Ps 18:2). YHWH is the mountain stronghold of the saint.
webster_summary: Hebrew "fortress" — the mountain stronghold; YHWH as fastness.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for fortress, specifically a mountain stronghold — a heavily-fortified high place difficult to assault. David's wilderness years were spent in literal metsudoth; he then turned the language toward YHWH in his psalms: "the LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer" (Ps 18:2). The masada (related word) at the Dead Sea is a real example.
scriptures: Psalm 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
Psalm 31:3
For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name's sake lead me, and guide me.
Psalm 91:2
I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.
corruption_summary: Modern "fortress" suggests military-history museum piece; the active-stronghold-of-the-saint sense has dimmed.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "fortress" is castle-tour vocabulary. Hebrew metsudah is active stronghold — the place from which to fight, the place that cannot be taken, the place where the king is safe. David lived in literal ones; we live in YHWH the spiritual fortress.
Recover the height: metsudah is not just walls but height. The fortress is on the mountain. To trust YHWH is to take the high ground.
usage: Metsudah is mountain stronghold.
Take the high ground in YHWH.
David's hiding place became David's hymn.

etymology: Hebrew yeshuah (יְשׁוּעָה), feminine of yesha, from yasha (to save). The name Yeshua (Jesus) is the masculine form — "YHWH saves."
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for salvation. Concrete and active — deliverance from real enemies, real disease, real captivity, and ultimately from sin. The proper name Jesus (Yeshua) is built on this root: "thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins" (Matt 1:21).
webster_summary: Hebrew "salvation" — concrete deliverance; the root of Jesus' name.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for salvation. Concrete and active — deliverance from enemies, from disease, from captivity, from sin. The masculine form of the same root, Yeshua, is the proper name Jesus — YHWH saves. Every utterance of "Jesus" is the gospel-promise that YHWH delivers His people.
scriptures: Exodus 15:2
The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation.
Psalm 27:1
The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
Matthew 1:21
And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.
corruption_summary: Spiritualized away from concrete deliverance; the OT salvation is real-enemy-real-rescue, prefiguring Christ's comprehensive saving.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christianity often spiritualizes salvation entirely — soul-only, future-only. OT yeshuah is concrete: rescue from Pharaoh, from Goliath, from disease, from captivity. The same God who delivered then delivers now — ultimately from sin in Christ, but also in real circumstances day by day.
Recover the concreteness: Yeshua means YHWH saves — from enemies, from disease, from despair, from sin. All of it is yeshuah.
usage: Yeshuah is concrete deliverance.
Yeshua / Jesus is the name that names the verb.
YHWH saves — from sin and from circumstance.

etymology: Hebrew avodah (עֲבוֹדָה), from avad (to work, serve, worship).
biblical_def: The Hebrew word that fuses work, service, and worship into one concept. Avodah is what the priests did in the tabernacle (worship), what slaves did in Egypt (forced work), and what the saint does in service to YHWH (worship-as-life). Hebrew refuses the modern distinction between sacred and secular labor.
webster_summary: Hebrew word that fuses work, service, and worship into one.
webster_full: A profoundly integrative Hebrew word that means simultaneously work, service, and worship. Avodah in the tabernacle is priestly service; avodah in Egypt is the slaves' forced labor; avodah of the saint is worship rendered as life. The Hebrew refuses the modern split between sacred and secular labor — all of it is avodah, oriented toward YHWH or against Him.
scriptures: Exodus 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage (avodah), in mortar, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field.
Joshua 24:15
And if it seem evil unto you to serve (avad) the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve.
Romans 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
corruption_summary: Modern split between work (secular) and worship (Sunday) misses the Hebrew unity of avodah.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christianity often inherits Greek-Latin splits: work is secular, worship is religious, service is volunteering. Hebrew avodah refuses the split. Slaves' forced work, priests' tabernacle ministry, and the saint's daily labor are all avodah — rendered to a master (Pharaoh, idol, or YHWH).
Recover the integration: every job is avodah. The question is not whether you're working or worshiping — you're always both. The question is whom you serve.
usage: Avodah fuses work, service, and worship.
Every job is rendered to some master.
Choose you this day whom ye will serve.

etymology: Hebrew kohen (כֹּהֵן) — one who stands before God on behalf of others; mediator.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for priest. The kohen mediates between God and people, offering sacrifices and pronouncing blessing. Aaron's line was set apart as kohanim under the old covenant. Christ is the High Kohen of the new covenant after the order of Melchizedek (Heb 7), and all believers are kohanim in the priesthood of all believers (1 Pet 2:9).
webster_summary: Hebrew "priest" — one who stands before God on behalf of others.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for priest. The kohen stands between God and people, offering sacrifice and pronouncing blessing. The Aaronic priesthood under the old covenant; Christ as the High Kohen after Melchizedek's order under the new covenant; and all believers as kohanim in the priesthood of all believers, declared at Sinai (Exod 19:6) and reaffirmed at Pentecost (1 Pet 2:9).
scriptures: Exodus 19:6
And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.
1 Peter 2:9
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him.
Hebrews 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
corruption_summary: Either narrowed to clergy (Roman Catholic / Anglican usage) or dropped entirely (low-church abandonment of priesthood-of-believers).
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors: clergy-only priesthood (the laity reduced to spectators) and no-priesthood-at-all (the laity reduced to consumers). Scripture insists on the priesthood of all believers — every saint a kohen, mediating Christ to the world by intercession, witness, and blessing.
Recover both: there are appointed elders/pastors (a specific function), but every believer is a kohen. We pray for each other, declare God's praises, and pronounce blessing in His name.
usage: Every believer is a kohen.
Christ is High Kohen after Melchizedek.
Mediate, intercede, bless — the kohen's work.

etymology: Hebrew melek (מֶלֶךְ) — king, ruler. The compound title Melek HaMelakim means King of Kings.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for king. Israel's true king is YHWH; the human king (David's line) reigns as YHWH's vassal. Christ is Melek HaMelakim — King of Kings (Rev 19:16). The kingdom theme runs from Eden's mandate through Davidic covenant to Christ's eschatological reign.
webster_summary: Hebrew "king" — YHWH first; David's line; Christ ultimately.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for king. The Old Testament's king-theology develops in stages: YHWH alone is Israel's king at first (1 Sam 8:7); under pressure Israel demands a human king "like the nations"; Saul fails; David's line is given the eternal covenant; the prophets foretell the ideal Davidic Son; Christ is revealed as Melek HaMelakim (Rev 19:16). The kingdom theme is Scripture's spine.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 8:7
And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them.
Psalm 24:7-8
Lift up your heads, O ye gates... and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty.
Revelation 19:16
And he hath on his vesture and on his thigh a name written, KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS.
corruption_summary: Democratic-age sensibilities recoil from kingship; the kingdom-of-God language gets soft-pedaled or replaced with kinder imagery.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern democracies have made "king" sound oppressive — the absolute ruler unaccountable to the governed. Scripture's kingship is different: the king under whom you flourish, the king who lays down His life for the kingdom. "King of Kings" is gospel, not threat.
Recover the kingship: Christ is melek. He reigns. The saint lives now under His reign and looks for the day when His reign is universally manifest. Kingdom-Christianity is biblical-Christianity.
usage: Melek HaMelakim — King of Kings.
YHWH is Israel's first King.
Recover kingdom-Christianity.

etymology: Hebrew nabi (נָבִיא) — one who speaks for another; spokesman; prophet.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for prophet. The nabi is YHWH's spokesman — one who declares God's word to the people, often calling them back from idolatry to covenant faithfulness. Christ is the prophet "like unto Moses" (Deut 18:15); the Spirit pours out the prophetic gift on all flesh at Pentecost (Joel 2; Acts 2).
webster_summary: Hebrew "prophet" — YHWH's spokesman.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for prophet. The nabi stands as YHWH's mouth — declaring His word, often confronting kings and nations, calling Israel back to covenant. Distinct from foreign diviners (the roeh [seer] is the older term; nabi is the standard from Samuel onward). Christ is the prophet like Moses; Pentecost democratizes the prophetic Spirit ("sons and daughters shall prophesy," Joel 2:28).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 18:15
The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken.
Amos 3:7
Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.
Joel 2:28
And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.
corruption_summary: Two errors: (1) prophets reduced to fortune-tellers; (2) the prophetic gift dismissed as ceased entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: Prophets aren't fortune-tellers. The biblical prophet's primary work is forth-telling (declaring God's word) more than fore-telling (predicting). Amos and Hosea spoke mostly to their own day. The prediction-element exists but is secondary.

And while the foundational apostolic-prophetic office is past (Eph 2:20), the broader prophetic Spirit poured out at Pentecost continues. Sons and daughters still prophesy — bring God's word to bear on their day.
usage: Nabi is forth-telling, not just fore-telling.
Christ is the Prophet like Moses.
Pentecost democratized the prophetic Spirit.

etymology: Hebrew qadosh (קָדוֹשׁ), from qadash (to be set apart, separate, consecrated).
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for holy — literally "set apart." YHWH's primary self-revelation: "holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6:3) names His total otherness from creation. Israel is to be qadosh because YHWH is qadosh (Lev 19:2). Holiness is set-apartness for God, not generic moral excellence.
webster_summary: Hebrew "holy" — set apart, separate, consecrated.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for holy. Literally "set apart, separate." YHWH's primary self-revelation in Isaiah 6 (the seraphim's threefold cry) and Revelation 4 names Him as qadosh. Holiness is not first moral excellence but ontological otherness — God is utterly distinct from creation, set apart from all His works. Israel is to be qadosh because YHWH is qadosh.
scriptures: Isaiah 6:3
And one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.
Leviticus 19:2
Speak unto all the congregation of the children of Israel, and say unto them, Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy.
But as he which hath called you is holy, so be ye holy in all manner of conversation; Because it is written, Be ye holy; for I am holy.
corruption_summary: Reduced to moral cleanness or pious behavior; the ontological set-apartness that makes morality possible drops out.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern Christianity often equates holy with morally good. Hebrew qadosh is more fundamental: God is utterly other. Moral excellence flows from His holiness, but the holiness is not reducible to morality. He is qadosh because He is God; we are to be qadosh because He has set us apart for Himself.
Recover the otherness: holiness is the burning bush, the consuming fire, the trembling of the seraphim. Awe before this is the beginning.
usage: Qadosh is set-apart-ness, not just moral cleanness.
Holy, holy, holy — the seraphim's threefold awe.
Be holy because He is holy.

etymology: Hebrew berakah (בְּרָכָה), from barak (to bless, to kneel) — possibly originally the kneeling-act associated with blessing.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for blessing. Berakah can flow from God to humans (covenant favor and increase) and from humans to God (acclaim and praise). The Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 is the great berakah; the patriarchal blessings in Genesis transfer covenant favor down generations.
webster_summary: Hebrew "blessing" — covenant favor, two-way (to and from God).
webster_full: The Hebrew word for blessing. Goes both directions: God blesses humans (covenant favor, increase, peace) and humans bless God (acknowledging His worth and giving thanks). The Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 is the great priestly berakah pronounced over Israel; patriarchal blessings (Isaac to Jacob, Jacob to his sons) transfer covenant favor down generations.
scriptures: Numbers 6:24-26
The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.
Genesis 12:2-3
And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing... and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
Psalm 103:1-2
Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits.
corruption_summary: Reduced to material prosperity ("#blessed" hashtag culture) or to mild well-wishing ("have a blessed day"); the covenantal weight thinned.
corruption_paragraphs: Social-media "blessed" usually means "successful" or "having a good day." Hebrew berakah is heavier: covenant favor that flows down generations, peace that surpasses understanding, peace pronounced authoritatively by the priest. Not a hashtag.
Recover the weight: pronouncing blessing is a priestly act. Receiving blessing is covenant inheritance. Both directions matter — bless the LORD, and be blessed by Him.
usage: Berakah flows two directions: to and from God.
Pronounce blessing; do not just wish it.
Bless the LORD, O my soul.

etymology: Hebrew tehillah (תְּהִלָּה), from halal (to praise, shine, be radiant). The Book of Psalms in Hebrew is Tehillim — "Praises."
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for praise — specifically sung, declared, public praise. From halal, which gives us hallelujah ("praise YHWH"). The Book of Psalms is Tehillim — "Praises." Tehillah is what the saint owes God for who He is and what He has done.
webster_summary: Hebrew "praise" — sung, declared, public.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for praise, especially the public, sung, declared kind. Derived from halal (to praise, to shine), which also gives hallelujah. The Book of Psalms in Hebrew is Tehillim — "Praises" — the worship-songbook of God's people. Tehillah is owed for who God is (His character) and what He has done (His acts).
scriptures: Psalm 33:1
Rejoice in the LORD, O ye righteous: for praise is comely for the upright.
Psalm 22:3
But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises (tehillah) of Israel.
Isaiah 61:3
To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise (tehillah) for the spirit of heaviness.
corruption_summary: Reduced to a single song-style or genre; the comprehensive declared-praise force of tehillah gets thinned.
corruption_paragraphs: "Praise music" in modern usage often means a particular genre. Hebrew tehillah is broader: anything declared aloud about God's character or works. The Psalter is full of laments, complaints, imprecations, confessions, thanksgivings — all of it tehillah, because all of it declares God truthfully.
Recover the breadth: God inhabits the praises of Israel (Ps 22:3). Where He is publicly declared, He is enthroned. The garment of praise replaces the spirit of heaviness.
usage: Tehillah is declared, public praise.
Hallelujah — praise YHWH.
He inhabits the praises of Israel.

etymology: Hebrew todah (תּוֹדָה), from yadah (to give thanks, confess) — same root as the tribal name Judah ("praise").
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for thanksgiving. Specifically a public, often sacrificial, declaration of God's deliverance — "I was in trouble; God delivered me; here is my thanks-offering." The todah sacrifice (Lev 7:12) was a peace offering of thanks. Modern Hebrew uses todah as the everyday word for "thanks."
webster_summary: Hebrew "thanksgiving" — public declaration of deliverance.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for thanksgiving. Specifically public, often sacrificial declaration of God's deliverance — the saint says aloud what God has done for them and offers thanks. The todah sacrifice (Lev 7:12-15) was a peace offering of gratitude. Same root as yadah (to confess) and the tribal name Judah ("praise"). In modern Hebrew, todah is everyday "thanks."
scriptures: Psalm 50:14
Offer unto God thanksgiving (todah); and pay thy vows unto the most High.
Psalm 100:4
Enter into his gates with thanksgiving (todah), and into his courts with praise (tehillah): be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
Leviticus 7:12
If he offer it for a thanksgiving, then he shall offer with the sacrifice of thanksgiving unleavened cakes mingled with oil.
corruption_summary: Reduced to private mental gratitude or seasonal observance (Thanksgiving holiday); the public-declaration force of todah thinned.
corruption_paragraphs: Gratitude-journaling is private mental thanksgiving — better than nothing, but not yet todah. Hebrew todah is public declaration: I was in trouble, He delivered me, here is the proof, here is the offering. Tell the room what He did.
Recover the publicness: enter His gates with todah. Sing it. Bring an offering. Tell others. Private gratitude becomes biblical thanksgiving when it becomes spoken declaration.
usage: Todah is public declaration, not private mental gratitude.
Enter His gates with thanksgiving.
Tell the room what He did.

etymology: Hebrew zera (זֶרַע) — seed, offspring, descendant.
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for seed, with a vast biblical sweep: the seed of the woman who would crush the serpent's head (Gen 3:15), the seed of Abraham through whom nations would be blessed (Gen 12:7), the seed of David from whom Messiah would come, and finally Christ Himself, the singular seed Paul identifies in Galatians 3:16.
webster_summary: Hebrew "seed" — offspring; covenant promise across generations.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for seed, used both literally (agricultural) and figuratively (offspring, descendants). Theologically loaded across Scripture: seed of the woman (Gen 3:15), seed of Abraham (Gen 12:7), seed of David (2 Sam 7:12), and supremely Christ as the seed (Paul's exegesis in Gal 3:16, where the singular zera — "and to thy seed, which is Christ"). The covenant runs through the seed.
scriptures: Genesis 3:15
And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
Galatians 3:16
Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made. He saith not, And to seeds, as of many; but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ.
Genesis 22:18
And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice.
corruption_summary: Lost as a theological category; modern readers miss the cumulative seed-thread that runs from Eden to Calvary.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations sometimes render zera as "offspring" or "descendants," which is accurate but loses the singular-collective ambiguity Paul exploits in Galatians 3:16. The seed promise narrows across Scripture: woman's seed, Abraham's seed, David's seed, the seed — Christ.
Recover the thread: Genesis 3:15 plants it; Genesis 12 names it; Genesis 22 confirms it; 2 Samuel 7 narrows it; the gospels reveal it. The seed-of-the-woman is Christ.
usage: Zera runs the covenant from Eden to Calvary.
The singular seed is Christ (Gal 3:16).
Read Genesis 3:15 as the gospel's first promise.

etymology: Hebrew berit (בְּרִית) — covenant, treaty, agreement; possibly from a root meaning "to cut" (covenants were ratified by cutting animals, Gen 15).
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for covenant. Across Scripture, YHWH binds Himself to His people through a series of beritot: with Noah (creation-preservation), Abraham (election), Moses (law), David (kingship), and the New Covenant (heart-renewal in Christ). "To cut a covenant" recalls the bisected animals Abraham walked between (Gen 15) — the sworn pledge sealed in blood.
webster_summary: Hebrew "covenant" — sworn binding agreement, often blood-ratified.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for covenant — the sworn binding agreement that structures all of Scripture's theology. Possibly from a root meaning "to cut," because covenants were ratified by cutting animals and walking between them (Gen 15). YHWH's berits with Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, and the New Covenant in Christ run as the thread of redemptive history. The Bible is structured into Old and New Berit (Testament = covenant).
scriptures: Genesis 15:18
In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land.
Jeremiah 31:31-33
Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah... I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts.
Luke 22:20
This cup is the new testament (berit) in my blood, which is shed for you.
corruption_summary: Reduced to vague agreement or contractual relationship; the blood-sworn, generational, life-and-death weight of berit thins.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern "covenant" sounds like a fancy contract. Hebrew berit is heavier: animals cut, blood spilled, oaths sworn, generations bound. "Cut a covenant" was literal. To break covenant was to invite the animal's fate.
Recover the weight: every covenant in Scripture is blood-sworn. The New Covenant is sealed in Christ's own blood. The wine at the Lord's Supper isn't symbol-of-symbol; it is the cup of the New Berit.
usage: Berit is blood-sworn binding.
Cut a covenant — the literal Hebrew picture.
The New Berit is sealed in Christ's blood.

etymology: Hebrew olam (עוֹלָם) — long duration, antiquity, eternity, age; literally "hidden distance."
biblical_def: The Hebrew word for eternity or age — the long duration that recedes beyond view. Used both backwards (me-olam, "from of old") and forwards (le-olam va'ed, "forever and ever"). YHWH is the El Olam, the Eternal God (Gen 21:33). The Hebrew word does not separate "eternity" from "age"; long duration is the concept.
webster_summary: Hebrew "eternity" / "age" — long duration receding beyond view.
webster_full: The Hebrew word for long duration, eternity, or age. Etymologically connected to the idea of "hidden distance" — the time-horizon that disappears from view in either direction. Used backwards (me-olam, from antiquity) and forwards (le-olam, forever). YHWH is named El Olam, the Everlasting God (Gen 21:33). The Hebrew refuses to separate eternity from age; both are duration beyond human perception.
scriptures: Genesis 21:33
And Abraham planted a grove in Beersheba, and called there on the name of the LORD, the everlasting God.
Psalm 90:2
Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
Isaiah 40:28
Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?
corruption_summary: Modern translations often render olam as "forever" or "eternal," losing the long-duration / horizon nuance.
corruption_paragraphs: Greek thinking gave us a sharp split between time and eternity. Hebrew olam doesn't split them — eternity is the duration that recedes beyond perception, in either direction. God is the El Olam because His durations span before-the-mountains and beyond-the-end-of-the-world.
Recover the horizon: olam is the curve of the earth where the road disappears. From olam to olam, the LORD is God.
usage: Olam is duration beyond perception.
El Olam — the Everlasting God.
From olam to olam, the LORD is God.
